FIG. 3. Zero-loop propagator at three times. (a) Regular part e−αtKt(x) of the p-adic propagator (32), computed from the explicit formula (F5) of Appendix F, for p = 2, N = 1, a kernel that is constant for |x|p ≤ 1 and decays as |x|−(1+σ)

FIG. 4. A regional network (Lemma 1) with four regions, K = ⊔3 a=0 B 1 −2(a), B 1 −2(a) = a + 4Z2 (p = 2, N = 1). Inside each region the kernel is constant, so the wavelet modes of region a relax at rate αa. The parameters are αa = (1, 1.2, 0.8, 1.5), f ′ a(0) = (1, 1.5, 0.8, 1.2) and f ′ a(0)ωa = (0.6, 0.7, 0.5, 0.9), and the interregional couplings are cab = ε d−2 ab , with dab = |a− b|2 ∈ {1/2, 1}. (a) The leading growth rate s(M) as a function of ε, and the band [−maxa µa,−mina µa] of Appendix E. The network is critical at εc ≈ 0.264, where µa ≈ (0.003,−0.095,−0.017, 0.124): the µa are not equal, so the critical dynamics is not conservative. (b) Regional activities Ua(t) at εc, with all activity initially in region 0. They converge to the Perron eigenvector of M and then stay constant. The total activity also tends to a constant, 1.07, different from its initial value 1.

FIG. 5. Avalanches at the critical point. (a) Probability that an avalanche has size at least S, for the hierarchical network with five values of σ and for a Euclidean chain with nearest-neighbor coupling. Dotted lines: the mean-field law S−1/2 (τS = 3/2) and the law S−0.108 of directed percolation in one dimension. (b) Avalanche-size exponent τS against σ. Filled circles: fit of the size distribution. Open squares: from the measured δ and ϑ. Cross: the Euclidean chain with nearest-neighbor coupling (simulated, fit of the size distribution); it has no parameter σ and is drawn to the right of the tree data. Dashed horizontal line: the value τS = 1.108 of directed percolation in one dimension [60], not a simulation. The vertical line marks σ = N/2, where N = Nc. Parameters as in Table II.

TABLE II. Simulation results at the critical point. bc: critical value of b = f ′(0)w0/α (mean-field value: 1). δ, ϑ: survival and growth exponents. τS (fit): maximum-likelihood fit of the size distribution; statistical errors are below 0.005. τS (scaling): from τS = 1+ δ/(1 + ϑ+ δ). In parentheses, the exact or known values of (δ, ϑ, τS) for the two controls: the critical branching process and DP in one dimension. The two controls show that the fitted τS is systematically too large by about 0.03.

TABLE III. Small-world tests for N = 1. C and ℓ: clustering coefficient and mean path length of the sparse network with n = 216 neurons. T1/2: spreading time of the spike model with n = 212 and n = 214 neurons, in units of 1/α. The sparse tree network with σ = 1.5 is not connected. A random graph of the same size and degree has C ≈ 10−4.

FIG. 6. Small-world tests. (a) Mean path length of sparse networks with n neurons, in which each neuron draws k = 6 connections with probabilities proportional to the coupling. Filled circles: tree with p = 2, N = 1 (the network with σ = 1.5 is not connected and is not shown). Open symbols: Euclidean ring with power-law coupling. Diamonds: Euclidean ring in which each neuron is connected to its five nearest neighbors on each side. (b) Spike model in the active phase, b = 6: mean time at which half of the n neurons have fired at least once, for the same networks; here the short-range ring has nearest-neighbor coupling. Error bars are standard errors and are mostly smaller than the symbols.

FIG. 7. Spectrum of the linearized dynamics (Sec. XB). Linearizing the Wilson–Cowan equation about the quiescent state gives ∂tu = −αu+ f ′(0)w ⋆u, whose eigenfunctions are the wavelets; a mode supported on balls of radius pγ grows at the rate ϱγ = −α+ f ′(0)ŵ(p1−γ) [Eq. (90)], so the first instability occurs where ŵ is largest. (a) p-adic theory: ŵ at each level γ, from Eq. (89), for p = 2, N = 1. Solid: a nonnegative kernel, constant for |x|p ≤ p−3 and decaying as |x|−2 p beyond; ŵ increases monotonically to its value w0 at the homogeneous mode (γ → ∞). Dashed: the same kernel with inhibitory (negative) coupling for |x|p ≥ p2; the maximum is at a finite level γc. (b) Euclidean theory: ŵ(q) for a Gaussian kernel and for a difference of Gaussians, whose maximum is at a nonzero wave number qc. In both theories a pattern-forming instability requires inhibition.
